content: 1. A post-intervention assessment was conducted at least 8 weeks after the baseline measurement. Independent evaluators analyzed participant characteristics, study design, methodological features, and intervention content. Summary effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. 2. A total of 23 studies involving 2,473 participants (mean age: 53 years; 43% women) met the eligibility criteria. Yoga was associated with significant improvements in glycemic outcomes, lipid profiles, blood pressure, body mass index, waist-to-hip ratio, and cortisol levels. 3. On average, the studies satisfied 41% of the methodological quality (MQ) criteria. However, the MQ score was not significantly associated with any outcomes (p > 0.05). Yoga demonstrated improvements in glycemic control and other risk factors for complications in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) compared to control conditions. 4. Further studies with longer follow-up periods are necessary to determine the long-term efficacy of yoga for adults with T2DM. Outcomes addressed included glycemic control, body composition, blood pressure, and lipid profiles. The population analyzed consisted of adults aged 18 years or older with a clinical diagnosis of T2DM. 5. Tai Chi interventions were evaluated for their effects on glucose control in patients with T2DM. Seventeen trials were included, and the results indicated that Tai Chi was effective in improving glycemic outcomes, particularly after durations exceeding 3 months. However, the evidence was insufficient to determine whether long-term Tai Chi training was more effective. 6. Tai Chi and Ba Duan Jin were identified as potentially effective options for improving biomedical and psychosocial well-being in individuals with T2DM. However, the evidence regarding their effects on blood pressure, waist circumference, and quality of life was inconclusive due to the limited number of studies. 7. Physical exercise, including aerobic and resistance training, was evaluated for its effects on inflammatory biomarkers and cardiopulmonary function in people living with HIV (PLWH). Twenty-three studies met the inclusion criteria, involving 1,073 participants aged 18–65 years. Exercise significantly improved cardiopulmonary function (VO2 max) but did not show significant effects on inflammatory biomarkers such as IL-6 and IL-1β. 8. Progressive resistance exercise (PRE) was assessed for its safety and effectiveness in adults living with HIV. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing PRE with no exercise or other interventions. PRE was found to improve strength, body composition, and psychological outcomes, but its effects on immunological and virological outcomes were less clear. 9. Moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (55–85% maximum heart rate) performed 2–5 times per week for 6–24 weeks significantly improved physical health-related quality of life in PLWH. However, there was no significant effect on CD4+ count or other quality-of-life domains. Evidence on the impact of exercise on bone mineral density in PLWH was lacking due to the paucity of randomized controlled trials. 10. The evidence suggests that further high-quality research is needed to explore the long-term effects of Tai Chi, the optimal intervention dose, and the impact of other traditional Chinese medicine-based lifestyle interventions on individuals with T2DM. Similarly, additional studies are required to clarify the effects of physical exercise on immune function, bone mineral density, and quality of life in PLWH.
